lessons.title: Greetings and Names

phrases.english: Where are you from? (to a man)
Where are you from? (to a woman)

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.english: Good, thank God. How are you?

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.arabic: أنا من حمص، بس ساكنة بدمشق.
dialogue.transliteration: ana min Homs, bas sakne b Dimashq.
dialogue.english: I'm from Homs, but I live in Damascus.

lessons.culture: In Damascus, greetings are often warm and repeated, especially when people meet after some time apart. Using a person's first name after an initial greeting is natural and friendly.

exercises.prompt: You are speaking to a man and he says: "مرحبا". Reply naturally.

too_formal.feedback: This is grammatically correct, but it is much more formal and elaborate than the everyday opening you need here.

exercises.tip: For a relaxed first greeting, "أهلا" or "أهلين" is very common.

exercises.prompt: A woman asks you: "كيفِك؟". Answer that you are doing well.

too_formal.feedback: The meaning is fine, but this sounds more formal and bookish than everyday Damascene speech.

exercises.tip: Use "منيحة" when a woman describes herself as well, and "منيح" when a man does.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence: "_____ رامي." English meaning: My name is Rami.

too_formal.feedback: This structure is much more formal than the simple spoken phrase used for introductions.

exercises.tip: The fixed everyday pattern is "اسمي + name".

exercises.prompt: Translate into Damascene Arabic: "What's your name?" when speaking to a man.

too_formal.feedback: This is understandable Arabic, but "شو اسمك؟" is the natural everyday Damascene choice.

exercises.tip: In Damascene speech, "شو" is a very common way to say "what".

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means "Where are you from?" when speaking to a woman?

too_formal.feedback: The sentence is correct, but it is more formal and specific than the ordinary conversational question.

exercises.tip: "إنتِ" marks the feminine singular in this question.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Nice to meet you."

too_formal.feedback: This is formal written-style Arabic. In conversation, "تشرفنا" is much more natural.

exercises.tip: "تشرفنا" is a useful fixed phrase for first meetings.

exercises.prompt: Someone says: "تشرفنا". Give a natural reply.

too_formal.feedback: That response is too elaborate for an ordinary first introduction.

exercises.tip: "وأنا كمان" is especially easy to use when you want a simple, friendly reply.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: "اسمك / شو".

too_formal.feedback: This is formal rather than the conversational Damascene pattern the exercise is practicing.

exercises.tip: Question word first is very natural here: "شو + اسمك؟"

exercises.prompt: Translate: "I'm from Damascus."

too_formal.feedback: This is correct, but adding "مدينة" makes it sound more explicit and formal than needed.

exercises.tip: For cities and countries, "أنا من + place" is the basic pattern.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "أنا من حلب، _____ ساكنة بدمشق." Meaning: I'm from Aleppo, but I live in Damascus.

too_formal.feedback: It is grammatical, but it is noticeably more formal than the everyday spoken connector "بس".

exercises.tip: "بس" is one of the most useful everyday words for "but".

exercises.prompt: Which reply fits "كيفك؟" most naturally?

too_formal.feedback: That wording is far too formal for an ordinary spoken exchange.

exercises.tip: A simple health check usually gets a short answer: "منيح" or "تمام".

exercises.prompt: You are a man. Someone asks: "من وين إنت؟" Say that you are from Damascus.

too_formal.feedback: This is far more formal than a natural introduction.

exercises.tip: You can answer with the full sentence or simply "من دمشق" when the context is clear.

lessons.title: Polite Everyday Requests

phrases.english: Can you help me? (to a man)
Can you help me? (to a woman)

dialogue.speaker: Tareq
dialogue.english: Excuse me, can you help me?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.english: Yes, of course. What do you need?

dialogue.speaker: Tareq
dialogue.english: Excuse me, where is the bathroom?

dialogue.speaker: Maya
dialogue.english: On the right, after the door.

pair.english: Excuse me, can you help me?

lessons.culture: In Damascene conversation, polite softeners such as "لو سمحت" and "معلش" are used very frequently, including in very ordinary situations. A brief "شكرا" followed by "عفوا" is completely natural.

exercises.prompt: You need help from a man. Start politely with "Excuse me, can you help me?"

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Damascene speech normally uses "فيك" and "لو سمحت".

exercises.tip: The spoken pattern is "لو سمحت + فيك...؟" when addressing a man.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Thank you very much."

too_formal.feedback: This is formal written Arabic. "شكرا كتير" is the natural conversational phrase.

exercises.tip: "كتير" can intensify thanks, praise, and many other everyday expressions.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "_____ سمحت، وين الحمّام؟"

too_formal.feedback: That wording is much more formal and uses a more formal term for bathroom.

exercises.tip: "لو سمحت" is a standard polite opener before a request.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase is a natural Damascene way to say "You're welcome"?

too_formal.feedback: This is understandable, but it is more formulaic and formal than the simple everyday "عفوا".

exercises.tip: "عفوا" works very naturally as the reply to "شكرا".

exercises.prompt: Someone says "شكرا" to you. Reply naturally.

too_formal.feedback: This is polite but noticeably more formal and ceremonial than the everyday replies.

exercises.tip: "ولا يهمك" is especially conversational and warm.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "I want some water."

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic. Damascene speech normally uses "بدي" for "I want".

exercises.tip: "بدي" is one of the core spoken patterns for wants and requests.

exercises.prompt: Which word means "Sorry" when the speaker is a man?

too_formal.feedback: This is correct, but it is more formal than the very common spoken "آسف".

exercises.tip: The final vowel changes with the speaker's gender: "آسف" for a man, "آسفة" for a woman.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Sorry, I didn't understand."

too_formal.feedback: That is formal Arabic. The spoken negative uses "ما" here.

exercises.tip: In this kind of everyday past-tense statement, "ما فهمت" is the natural colloquial form.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in a natural order: "تساعدني / فيك / لو سمحت".

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic rather than everyday Damascene phrasing.

exercises.tip: Put the polite opener first, then the spoken ability pattern "فيك + verb".

exercises.prompt: A woman asks you politely for help and says "لو سمحت، فيك تساعدني؟" Reply positively.

too_formal.feedback: This is warmer in a formal or service context, but it is much more elaborate than necessary in casual conversation.

exercises.tip: "إي، أكيد" is an easy, friendly yes.

exercises.prompt: Complete the reply: "شكرا." — "_____ ."

too_formal.feedback: It is acceptable Arabic, but it is more formal and less direct than the everyday reply.

exercises.tip: Keep the reply short; native conversation often does.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "It's okay / Don't worry."

too_formal.feedback: This is correct but sounds more formal than the common spoken "معلش".

exercises.tip: "معلش" can soften a small apology, reassure someone, or excuse a minor inconvenience.

lessons.title: Numbers, Time, and Simple Plans

phrases.english: We'll see you tomorrow. (to a man)
I'll see you tomorrow. (to a man)

dialogue.speaker: Abu Samer
dialogue.english: Yes, I have a little work.

dialogue.speaker: Nour
dialogue.english: Good. Shall we see you tomorrow?

lessons.culture: In casual Damascene speech, time is often discussed with simple whole-hour expressions rather than a full formal sentence. "بكرا" and "هلق" are especially common everyday words for planning and talking about the immediate future and present.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "What time is it?"

too_formal.feedback: This is correct, but the colloquial Damascene form usually uses "قديش".

exercises.tip: Use "قديش" for "how much/how many" in many everyday questions.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "It's two o'clock."

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic. The spoken Damascene number is commonly "تنين" or "اتنين".

exercises.tip: For casual speech, "تنين" is a very common spoken form of two.

exercises.prompt: Which word means "tomorrow"?

too_formal.feedback: This is standard formal Arabic; Damascene speech uses "بكرا".

exercises.tip: Remember the three basic time words: اليوم, هلق, بكرا.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "_____ فاضي." Meaning: I'm free tomorrow.

too_formal.feedback: This is formal and more explicit than the everyday Damascene sentence.

exercises.tip: Colloquial Arabic often lets the context make the pronoun clear.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks: "بكرا فاضي؟" Reply that you are free.

too_formal.feedback: This is much more formal than a natural spoken answer.

exercises.tip: A short "إي، فاضي" is enough when the question already gives the context.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Today I have a little work."

too_formal.feedback: This sounds like formal Arabic. Damascene uses "عندي" and "شغل" in casual speech.

exercises.tip: "عندي" is the everyday way to express possession or something you have to do.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural sentence: "بكرا / منشوفك".

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic. The spoken future here is built with "منشوفك".

exercises.tip: In colloquial speech, future meaning is often built directly into the verb form.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means "Now"?

too_formal.feedback: This is understandable, but it is more formal than the everyday Damascene "هلق".

exercises.tip: "هلق" is one of the most frequent everyday Syrian time words.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "See you tomorrow." when speaking to a man.

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic. The everyday Damascene form uses "بشوفك" or "منشوفك".

exercises.tip: "بشوفك" is a useful spoken phrase for saying that you will see someone.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "الساعة _____ مناسبة؟" Meaning: Is one o'clock suitable?

too_formal.feedback: This is grammatical, but the short spoken form "الساعة وحدة" is more natural in the dialogue style being practiced.

exercises.tip: When telling the time, the spoken form often drops the formal case ending.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Three."

too_formal.feedback: This is the standard form; Damascene speech commonly pronounces it as "تلاتة".

exercises.tip: Listen for the spoken shift from formal "ث" to the common Damascene pronunciation in words like "تلاتة".

exercises.prompt: Someone proposes meeting at one o'clock and asks if that works. Say yes.

too_formal.feedback: This is formal and unnecessarily elaborate for a simple scheduling exchange.

exercises.tip: Use "مناسبة" for a time that works for you.

lessons.title: Around Damascus

dialogue.speaker: Khaled
dialogue.english: Excuse me, where is the market?

dialogue.speaker: Dima
dialogue.english: Yes, then you'll see it on the left.

lessons.culture: Giving directions in Damascus is often conversational and incremental: a person may give one turn, wait for the listener to react, and then add the next step. "يعطيك العافية" is a very common warm expression of thanks, especially after someone helps you.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Where is the market?"

too_formal.feedback: This is standard Arabic. "وين السوق؟" is the natural colloquial Damascene form.

exercises.tip: "وين" is one of the first location words to learn for Syrian conversation.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase means "On the right"?

too_formal.feedback: This is much more formal and explicit than the normal spoken direction.

exercises.tip: The spoken form joins the preposition and noun: "عاليمين".

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Straight ahead."

too_formal.feedback: This is formal and sounds like written instructions rather than everyday speech.

exercises.tip: "دغري" is an extremely useful conversational word for going straight.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "لف _____ اليمين." Meaning: Turn right.

too_formal.feedback: This is unnecessarily formal for a simple spoken direction.

exercises.tip: In speech, "على + اليمين" commonly contracts to "عاليمين".

exercises.prompt: Someone asks whether the market is far. Tell them it is very close.

too_formal.feedback: This uses formal vocabulary and structure; the everyday reply is much shorter.

exercises.tip: "كتير" often follows an adjective to make it stronger: "قريب كتير".

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Here."

too_formal.feedback: It is understood, but "هون" is the standard everyday Damascene form.

exercises.tip: Learn the pair "هون" for here and "هنيك" for there.

exercises.prompt: Which word means "there"?

too_formal.feedback: This is standard Arabic; conversational Damascene uses "هنيك".

exercises.tip: "هنيك" points to a place away from the speaker.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in a natural order: "السوق / وين".

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic rather than the target colloquial pattern.

exercises.tip: A location question often starts with "وين".

exercises.prompt: Translate: "And then?"

too_formal.feedback: That is formal and much longer than the normal spoken question.

exercises.tip: "بعدين" is a very high-frequency conversational word meaning "then/later."

exercises.prompt: Someone thanks you with "يعطيك العافية". Give a natural reply.

too_formal.feedback: That is not the usual conversational response to this fixed expression.

exercises.tip: Match the gender of the person you are addressing: "يعافيك" to a man and "يعافيكي" to a woman.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase means "Turn left" when speaking to a man?

too_formal.feedback: This is formal Arabic. The everyday spoken imperative is "لف".

exercises.tip: The masculine imperative is "لف"; the feminine form is "لفّي".

exercises.prompt: Translate: "The market is near."

too_formal.feedback: The longer sentence is grammatical, but unnecessary when simply stating that the market is near.

exercises.tip: Simple adjective sentences can be very short in Damascene Arabic.

challenge.title: Your First Damascene Conversation
challenge.instructions: Write and say a short Damascene conversation that lasts at least 10 lines. It must include a greeting, asking and answering names, asking where someone is from, one polite request, one thank-you exchange, one question about a time, and one set of directions. Use at least 8 target phrases from Unit 1 and include both a masculine-address form and a feminine-address form.
required_elements: A natural greeting using مرحبا, أهلا, or أهلين.
A name question and a name answer.
A question using من وين and a place answer.
A polite request using لو سمحت or لو سمحتي.
A response using إي، أكيد or a natural equivalent.
A thank-you exchange using شكرا and عفوا or a natural equivalent.
A time question using الساعة قديش؟.
A future plan using بكرا or a similar target expression.
At least two direction phrases such as عاليمين, عاليسار, دغري, هون, or هنيك.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.arabic: أهلا، منيحة الحمد لله. إنت شو اسمك؟
dialogue.transliteration: ahleen, mnii7a il7amdella. enta shoo ismak?
dialogue.english: Hi, I'm good, thank God. What's your name?

dialogue.speaker: Samer
dialogue.english: My name is Samer. And you?

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.english: I'm Lina. Nice to meet you.

dialogue.speaker: Samer
dialogue.transliteration: w ana kaman. min ween enti?
dialogue.english: Me too. Where are you from?

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.arabic: أنا من حمص، بس ساكنة بدمشق.
dialogue.transliteration: ana min Homs, bas sakne b Dimashq.
dialogue.english: I'm from Homs, but I live in Damascus.

dialogue.speaker: Samer
dialogue.english: Excuse me, can you help me?

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.english: Yes, of course. What do you need?

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.arabic: من هون، امشي دغري وبعدين لف عاليمين.
dialogue.transliteration: min hoon, imshi deghri w ba3deen leff 3al-yamiin.
dialogue.english: From here, walk straight and then turn right.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.arabic: لا، قريب كتير. والساعة قديش بدك تروح؟
dialogue.transliteration: la, 2ariib ktiir. w is-saa3a addeesh baddak troo7?
dialogue.english: No, it's very close. And what time do you want to go?
